findings.claim: The two capturing groups in the exported `email` regex were converted to non-capturing groups, silently changing the shape of `exec()`/`match()` results for any consumer that reads capture groups or composes this pattern's `source` with numbered backreferences.
findings.rationale: Before: `([A-Za-z0-9_'+\-\.]*)` and `([A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9\-]*\.)+` were group 1 and group 2. After: both are `(?:...)`, so `email.exec(x)` now returns an array of length 1 instead of 3. Zod itself only uses `.test()` as far as I know, so this is likely harmless internally, but `email` is a publicly exported RegExp and `regexes.ts` patterns are also stitched into other patterns via `.source` in some places; any external code doing `zod/v4/core/regexes.email.exec(v)[1]` breaks. Medium confidence that it matters in practice, high confidence the behavior difference is real.

findings.claim: The new local-part pattern introduces overlapping quantifiers — `(?:[A-Za-z0-9_'+\-]+\.)*` followed by `[A-Za-z0-9_'+\-]*` and then `[A-Za-z0-9_+-]` (a subset of the preceding class) — which adds backtracking ambiguity on non-matching inputs that the old lookahead-based pattern did not have.
findings.rationale: Low confidence this is exploitable: the literal `\.` separator makes the outer star's split points deterministic (the class excludes `.`), and the trailing subset-class only costs one extra retry per stop position, so I believe worst-case work stays roughly linear/polynomial rather than exponential. Still worth a second look with a ReDoS checker since this regex is applied to untrusted user input by default, and the change removes the `(?!.*\.\.)` fast-fail guard that previously rejected many malformed inputs up front.
